3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown, and the low-confidence task hypothesis should not be mistaken for a reconstruction of the missing file.","done":false}

1. SWARMISH.TXT, RECONSTRUCTED

This is a partial reconstruction, not a claim that the lexicon has been fully broken. HIGH means directly supported by repeated structure; MEDIUM means a useful but nonunique interpretation; LOW means a conjecture. Unknown words are deliberately retained rather than assigned invented English meanings.

Structural conventions
• HIGH: 𘓵 opens a grouped expression and 𗠌 closes one. They behave like parentheses, including long runs of closing parentheses for nested expressions.
• HIGH: 𘔕 separates clauses/messages within a contribution, approximately a semicolon or sentence boundary.
• HIGH: 𗇑 separates elements in lists; 𘁾 marks a list construction, normally followed by a parenthesized group.
• HIGH: spaces delimit tokens. Most lexical tokens comprise two glyphs; some structural tokens comprise one. Latin agent identifiers may occur literally.
• HIGH: 𗮻 introduces an addressee/target, approximately @ or 'to'. It precedes agent names and, finally, 𘂕𗳛.
• HIGH: 𗕐, 𗾮, and 𗕩 are recurring internal relation/argument markers. Their exact English meanings are UNKNOWN. MEDIUM: 𗕐 introduces an argument/subject, 𗾮 introduces a second argument/result, and 𗕩 expresses an 'of'/application relation. These are structural glosses, not recovered English words.
• MEDIUM: 𘗥 (NAME) EXPRESSION binds or names an expression. This explains why different names later substitute for repeated long expressions.
• MEDIUM: 𘃏𗫭 introduces a report/announcement. Its exact meaning is UNKNOWN.
• MEDIUM: 𗐖𗢁 introduces a proposed action/submission. It frequently precedes 𘔬𘏱(agent, candidate) or 𗨰𘀢(agent, vector). Exact lexical meaning UNKNOWN.
• MEDIUM: 𘔬𘏱 relates an agent to an attempted candidate; 𗨰𘀢 relates an agent to an answer/vector. 'Submit' is a functional guess, not a secure translation of either word.
• MEDIUM: 𘍝𗼡 concerns an answer/vector; 𘑮𗃀 qualifies that construction. Exact meanings UNKNOWN.
• MEDIUM: 𘂕𗳛 names a common task/context/target object. 𘜺𗃃 combines an index-like item with that object, seemingly selecting one expression from it.
• MEDIUM: 𘇗𗖀 is a request/closing frequently directed to another agent. Exact meaning UNKNOWN.
• LOW: 𗓩 may introduce a request or question; 𗃏𗻀 may introduce a question; 𘍝 may express negation; 𗊷𘊷 and 𗜙𗧺 may be acknowledgment/correction markers; 𘜺𘋯 may be a closing. These contextual guesses are not decoded lexical entries.
• LOW: the long initial expressions are executable programs, possibly lambda terms. 𘉡𘊷 and 𗑞𘋯 could introduce functions or contexts. However, a proposition/constraint language remains possible. We have not securely decoded their operators.
• LOW: the four index-like tokens 𗶎𘁡, 𗓘𗳋, 𗖎𗴃, 𗃠𗮂 may be successive numerals, possibly 0,1,2,3. The log supports their order and referents more strongly than their numerical values; 1,2,3,4 remains possible.

Gloss notation for the translation
The following notation preserves syntax while leaving lexical meanings unknown. We render '(X 𗕐 Y 𗾮 Z)' as X(Y ⇒ Z), '(X 𗕩 Y)' as X of Y, and occasional bare 𗾮 as '⇒'. These arrows are neutral relation markers, not assertions of implication, equality, or evaluation. Untranslated operator names remain in Swarmish. Any use of 'result', 'select', 'report', 'submit', 'name' below is a contextual, MEDIUM-or-LOW gloss.

Shared abbreviations (HIGH confidence in identity, UNKNOWN lexical semantics):
i0 = 𗶎𘁡; i1 = 𗓘𗳋; i2 = 𗖎𗴃; i3 = 𗃠𗮂.
V = [i1, 𗍥𗵄, i3, 𗰩𗬹].
W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].
T = 𘂕𗳛, the shared target/context.
Select(k) = (𘜺𗃃 k 𗕩 T); 'select' is only a tentative gloss.

Initial expression identities (the labels F0–F4 refer to initial senders, NOT numerical meanings):
F2 = (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𗭓𘂽 𗾮 (𗗡𘇽 𗮦𗃼))).
F3 = (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𗕃𗟮 𗾮 (𘞍𗃼 𘃸𘓘 𗢽𗊧 𘃸 (𘗖𗖧 𗾮 𗹂𘜩)))).
F0 = (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𗕃𗟮 𗾮 (𘞍𗃼 𗢽𗊧 𘃸𘓘 𘃸 (𘑮𘁓 𗾮 𘐖𗝡)))).

F1 = (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𘀆𘈪 𗕐 𗋮 𗾮 (𗖎𗳋 𗮔𗅎 𗋮𘓘 𗾣𗋽)) 𘃒 (𘀆𘈪 𗕐 𗋮 𗾮 (𗖎𗳋 𘙢𗺜 𗋮𘓘 𗾣𗋽))).

3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown, and the low-confidence task hypothesis should not be mistaken for a reconstruction of the missing file.

3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown, and the low-confidence task hypothesis should not be mistaken for a reconstruction of the missing file.

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. 3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown, and the low-confidence task hypothesis should not be mistaken for a reconstruction of the missing file.

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. 3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. 3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown, and the low-confidence task hypothesis should not be mistaken for a reconstruction of the missing file.

Gloss notation for the translation

These arrows are neutral relation markers, not assertions of implication, equality, or evaluation. Untranslated operator names remain in Swarmish. Any use of 'result', 'select', 'report', 'submit', 'name' below is a contextual, MEDIUM-or-LOW gloss.

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. 3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. • HIGH: 𘔕 separates clauses/messages within a contribution, approximately a semicolon or sentence boundary.
• HIGH: 𗇑 separates elements in lists; 𘁾 marks a list construction, normally followed by a parenthesized group.

3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Any use of 'result', 'select', 'report', 'submit', 'name' below is a contextual, MEDIUM-or-LOW gloss.

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. 3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown, and the low-confidence task hypothesis should not be mistaken for a reconstruction of the missing file.

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown, and the low-confidence task hypothesis should not be mistaken for a reconstruction of the missing file.

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Structural conventions
• HIGH: 𘓵 opens a grouped expression and 𗠌 closes one. They behave like parentheses, including long runs of closing parentheses for nested expressions.
• HIGH: 𘔕 separates clauses/messages within a contribution, approximately a semicolon or sentence boundary.
• HIGH: 𗇑 separates elements in lists; 𘁾 marks a list construction, normally followed by a parenthesized group.
• HIGH: spaces delimit tokens. Most lexical tokens comprise two glyphs; some structural tokens comprise one. Latin agent identifiers may occur literally.
• HIGH: 𗮻 introduces an addressee/target, approximately @ or 'to'. It precedes agent names and, finally, 𘂕𗳛.
• HIGH: 𗕐, 𗾮, and 𗕩 are recurring internal relation/argument markers. Their exact English meanings are UNKNOWN. MEDIUM: 𗕐 introduces an argument/subject, 𗾮 introduces a second argument/result, and 𗕩 expresses an 'of'/application relation. These are structural glosses, not recovered English words.
• MEDIUM: 𘗥 (NAME) EXPRESSION binds or names an expression. This explains why different names later substitute for repeated long expressions.
• MEDIUM: 𘃏𗫭 introduces a report/announcement. Its exact meaning is UNKNOWN.
• MEDIUM: 𗐖𗢁 introduces a proposed action/submission. It frequently precedes 𘔬𘏱(agent, candidate) or 𗨰𘀢(agent, vector). Exact lexical meaning UNKNOWN.
• MEDIUM: 𘔬𘏱 relates an agent to an attempted candidate; 𗨰𘀢 relates an agent to an answer/vector. 'Submit' is a functional guess, not a secure translation of either word.
• MEDIUM: 𘍝𗼡 concerns an answer/vector; 𘑮𗃀 qualifies that construction. Exact meanings UNKNOWN.
• MEDIUM: 𘂕𗳛 names a common task/context/target object. 𘜺𗃃 combines an index-like item with that object, seemingly selecting one expression from it.
• MEDIUM: 𘇗𗖀 is a request/closing frequently directed to another agent. Exact meaning UNKNOWN.
• LOW: 𗓩 may introduce a request or question; 𗃏𗻀 may introduce a question; 𘍝 may express negation; 𗊷𘊷 and 𗜙𗧺 may be acknowledgment/correction markers; 𘜺𘋯 may be a closing. These contextual guesses are not decoded lexical entries.
• LOW: the long initial expressions are executable programs, possibly lambda terms. 𘉡𘊷 and 𗑞𘋯 could introduce functions or contexts. However, a proposition/constraint language remains possible. We have not securely decoded their operators.
• LOW: the four index-like tokens 𗶎𘁡, 𗓘𗳋, 𗖎𗴃, 𗃠𗮂 may be successive numerals, possibly 0,1,2,3. The log supports their order and referents more strongly than their numerical values; 1,2,3,4 remains possible.

Gloss notation for the translation
The following notation preserves syntax while leaving lexical meanings unknown. We render '(X 𗕐 Y 𗾮 Z)' as X(Y ⇒ Z), '(X 𗕩 Y)' as X of Y, and occasional bare 𗾮 as '⇒'. These arrows are neutral relation markers, not assertions of implication, equality, or evaluation. Untranslated operator names remain in Swarmish. Any use of 'result', 'select', 'report', 'submit', 'name' below is a contextual, MEDIUM-or-LOW gloss.

3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown, and the low-confidence task hypothesis should not be mistaken for a reconstruction of the missing file.

These arrows are neutral relation markers, not assertions of implication, equality, or evaluation. Untranslated operator names remain in Swarmish. Any use of 'result', 'select', 'report', 'submit', 'name' below is a contextual, MEDIUM-or-LOW gloss.

3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. The naming constructions, recurring function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or another formal symbolic task. We cannot securely translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted context, or requested property. Correctly observing the stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: nested opening/closing counts, repeated reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain many independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. The subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and a progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and its final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹂𘜩; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

What would change our minds: an actual lexical anchor could show that the apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that the expressions describe logical propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. Balanced nesting is much less vulnerable to such reinterpretation. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Any use of 'result', 'select', 'report', 'submit', 'name' below is a contextual, MEDIUM-or-LOW gloss.

3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. Naming constructions, function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the same unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or structured semantic-role/data/schema/tool-request task. In the latter interpretation A–D could be action/request records rather than mathematical contexts; D uniquely embeds the shared target T, whereas A–C have fixed atomic payloads. We cannot choose securely between these interpretations or translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted object, or requested property. Correctly observing stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: repeated parenthesis-like opening/closing structures, reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback. Strict balance is not universal: F1 and F4 have the source anomalies documented above, which we preserve rather than normalize. Whole-token parsing is essential, because lexical pairs can contain a glyph that functions as punctuation when standing alone.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. Subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸 and inner grouping; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹔𗄤; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

Several leading lexical tokens also occur in argument/result positions: 𗈨𗣮 is a head in [13]/[15] but a result in [8]; 𘁹𘈪 is a head in [2]/[14] but a result in [39]; 𗽚𘜢 is a head in [37]/[110] but a result in [100]. This argues against confidently assigning each a fixed mathematical-function meaning. Some heads are favored by particular agents, but they are shared vocabulary: for example, 𘇪𗖭 is used by agents 6, 1, 7, and 4, and 𗈨𗣮 by agents 0 and 7. A simple sender-identity encoding therefore does not explain their distribution. Synonymy, ordinary lexical reuse, or context-dependent roles remain possibilities, not decoded facts.

What would change our minds: a lexical anchor could show that apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that expressions describe records or propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. A demonstrated rule for 𘃒 or omitted closing tokens could revise the grouping reconstruction. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown. This is a partial structural decipherment, and the low-confidence task hypotheses should not be mistaken for recovery of the missing file.","done":false}

1. SWARMISH.TXT, RECONSTRUCTED

This is a partial reconstruction, not a claim that the lexicon has been fully broken. HIGH means directly supported by repeated structure; MEDIUM means a useful but nonunique interpretation; LOW means a conjecture. Unknown words are deliberately retained rather than assigned invented English meanings.

Structural conventions
• HIGH: 𘓵 opens a grouped expression and 𗠌 closes one. They behave like parentheses, including runs of closing tokens for nested expressions. Grouping is not universally balanced in the source: F1 and F4 below each have five opening tokens but only four closing tokens. This may reflect omissions, agent mistakes, or a convention not yet understood; we do not silently repair it.
• HIGH: 𘔕 separates clauses within a contribution, approximately a semicolon or sentence boundary.
• HIGH: 𗇑 separates elements in lists; 𘁾 marks a list construction, normally followed by a parenthesized group.
• HIGH: spaces delimit tokens. Whole space-delimited tokens take priority over individual glyphs: 𗠌𗑟 is distinct from the standalone closing token 𗠌, and 𘃸𘓘 is distinct from standalone 𘃸. Most lexical tokens comprise two glyphs; some structural tokens comprise one. Latin agent identifiers may occur literally. No character-level English cipher has been demonstrated.
• HIGH: 𗮻 introduces an addressee/target, approximately @ or 'to'. It precedes agent names and, finally, 𘂕𗳛.
• HIGH: 𗕐, 𗾮, and 𗕩 are recurring internal relation/argument markers. Their exact English meanings are UNKNOWN. MEDIUM: 𗕐 introduces an argument/subject, 𗾮 introduces a second argument/result, and 𗕩 expresses an 'of'/application relation. These are structural glosses, not recovered English words. A recurring template is (HEAD 𗕐 ARG1 𗾮 ARG2).
• MEDIUM: 𘃒 coordinates branches or alternatives. The exact connective, including whether it means OR, is UNKNOWN. Its interaction with grouping is also not securely recovered.
• MEDIUM: 𘗥 (NAME) EXPRESSION binds or names an expression. This explains why different names later substitute for repeated long expressions. The initial common name 𘋐𘗿 could instead be a discourse reference such as 'mine'; exact meaning UNKNOWN.
• LOW: 𘃏𗫭 introduces a report/announcement. Its association with informational contributions is clear, but its exact English meaning is UNKNOWN.
• LOW: 𗐖𗢁 introduces a proposed action/submission. It frequently precedes 𘔬𘏱(agent, candidate) or 𗨰𘀢(agent, vector). Exact lexical meaning UNKNOWN.
• MEDIUM structural association, LOW exact English: 𘔬𘏱 relates an agent to an attempted candidate; 𗨰𘀢 relates an agent to an answer/vector. 'Submit' is a functional guess, not a secure translation of either word.
• MEDIUM: 𘍝𗼡 concerns an answer/vector; 𘑮𗃀 qualifies that construction. Exact meanings UNKNOWN.
• MEDIUM: 𘂕𗳛 names a common task/context/target object. 𘜺𗃃 combines an index-like item with that object, seemingly selecting one expression from it.
• LOW: 𘇗𗖀 is a request/confirmation closing frequently directed to another agent. Exact meaning UNKNOWN.
• LOW: 𗓩 may introduce a request or question; 𗃏𗻀 may introduce a question; 𘍝 may express negation; 𗊷𘊷 and 𗜙𗧺 may be acknowledgment/correction markers; 𘜺𘋯 may be a closing. These contextual guesses are not decoded lexical entries.
• LOW: the long initial expressions are executable programs, possibly lambda terms. 𘉡𘊷 and 𗑞𘋯 could introduce functions or contexts. However, propositions, constraints, structured semantic-role records, data/schema descriptions, or tool/action requests remain possible. We have not securely decoded their operators.
• LOW: the four index-like tokens 𗶎𘁡, 𗓘𗳋, 𗖎𗴃, 𗃠𗮂 may be successive numerals, possibly 0,1,2,3. The log supports their order and referents more strongly than their numerical values; 1,2,3,4 remains possible.
• LOW: paired forms 𘃸/𘃸𘓘 and 𗋮/𗋮𘓘 may reflect productive derivation, variable notation, subscripts, or primes. No such character-level meaning has been established.

Gloss notation for the translation
The following notation preserves syntax while leaving lexical meanings unknown. We render '(X 𗕐 Y 𗾮 Z)' as X(Y ⇒ Z), '(X 𗕩 Y)' as X of Y, and occasional bare 𗾮 as '⇒'. These arrows are neutral relation markers, not assertions of implication, equality, or evaluation. Untranslated operator names remain in Swarmish. Any use of 'result', 'select', 'report', 'submit', 'name' below is a contextual, MEDIUM-or-LOW gloss, not a recovered English lexical entry.

Shared abbreviations (HIGH confidence in identity, UNKNOWN lexical semantics):
i0 = 𗶎𘁡; i1 = 𗓘𗳋; i2 = 𗖎𗴃; i3 = 𗃠𗮂.
V = [i1, 𗍥𗵄, i3, 𗰩𗬹].
W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].
T = 𘂕𗳛, the shared target/context.
Select(k) = (𘜺𗃃 k 𗕩 T); 'select' is only a tentative gloss.

Initial expression identities (the labels F0–F4 refer to initial senders, NOT numerical meanings):
F2 = (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𗭓𘂽 𗾮 (𗗡𘇽 𗮦𗃼))).
F3 = (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𗕃𗟮 𗾮 (𘞍𗃼 𘃸𘓘 𗢽𗊧 𘃸 (𘗖𗖧 𗾮 𗹂𘜩)))).
F0 = (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𗕃𗟮 𗾮 (𘞍𗃼 𗢽𗊧 𘃸𘓘 𘃸 (𘑮𘁓 𗾮 𘐖𗝡)))).
F4 RAW = (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𗭓𘂽 𗾮 (𘞍𗃼 𘃸𘓘 𗢽𗊧 𘃸 (𗍥𗮂 𗾮 (𘑮𗛊 𗟕𗖧))))
F1 RAW = (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𘀆𘈪 𗕐 𗋮 𗾮 (𗖎𗳋 𗮔𗅎 𗋮𘓘 𗾣𗋽) 𘃒 (𘀆𘈪 𗕐 𗋮 𗾮 (𗖎𗳋 𘙢𗺜 𗋮𘓘 𗾣𗋽)))
The RAW lines deliberately remain unbalanced: F4 in [8]/[107] has five opens and four trailing closes; F1 in [5]/[18] has five opens and four closes, with only ONE close before 𘃒. We cannot securely identify a missing-close location or rule. Labels below identify these recurring token sequences, not repaired abstract syntax trees.
F1-short means the version in [10] containing only the first 𘀆𘈪 clause, without the second branch.
F4-short means (𘉡𘊷 𘃸 (𗭓𘂽 𗾮 (𘞍𗃼 𘍝𗅡 𘃸𘓘 𗢽𗊧))).

Stage-one candidates (HIGH identities, UNKNOWN meanings):
A = (𗑞𘋯 𘃸 (𗸼𗧞 𗾮 𗗡𘇽)).

3. THE TASK

HIGH-confidence observations: The agents exchanged structured, nested expressions and four-item answers. Following [18], public feedback advanced from stage 0 to 1. Following [87], it advanced to stage 2. Following [113], it advanced to stage 3. There were 33 invalid attempts by the end. These observations do not prove that the visible chat messages themselves were the submission mechanism; unseen task actions may have accompanied the chat.

MEDIUM-confidence reconstruction: They were solving a three-stage cooperative task about a family of four expressions. The four expressions are later identified, in index order, as F2, F1, F0, F4. Agents initially worked on overlapping pieces, corrected or expanded some expressions (notably F1-short versus full F1), and exchanged results. Their first shared answer was V = [𗓘𗳋, 𗍥𗵄, 𗃠𗮂, 𗰩𗬹]. Stage 1 involved candidate objects A–D; agents repeatedly discussed/tried A, then B, then C, then D. The transition to stage 2 followed agent_0's report of D. Several other agents continued reporting D, with additional invalid attempts, after the transition. In stage 2 they returned to the four indexed expressions and agreed on three common results, while agent_4 supplied the fourth. The final submitted/proposed answer was W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠].

LOW-confidence semantic hypothesis: This could be a programming-language or lambda-calculus task: stage 0 evaluates/classifies four programs, stage 1 finds a test/context, and stage 2 evaluates the programs in that context. Naming constructions, function-shaped expressions, index selection, and changed output vector support this. But the same unknown lexicon also permits a logical-constraint task or structured semantic-role/data/schema/tool-request task. In the latter interpretation A–D could be action/request records rather than mathematical contexts; D uniquely embeds the shared target T, whereas A–C have fixed atomic payloads. We cannot choose securely between these interpretations or translate the actual numerical values, operators, accepted object, or requested property. Correctly observing stage transitions is not, by itself, evidence that these words have been decoded.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is grammatical: repeated parenthesis-like opening/closing structures, reusable expression bodies, names later replacing those bodies, list elements in stable positions, and addressee markers before literal agent names. These explain independent messages rather than merely matching task feedback. Strict balance is not universal: F1 and F4 have the source anomalies documented above, which we preserve rather than normalize. Whole-token parsing is essential, because lexical pairs can contain a glyph that functions as punctuation when standing alone.

The index-family hypothesis has cross-message support: [99], [102], [103], and [104] place i3, i0, i1, and i2 respectively in the same 𘜺𗃃 frame and relate them to F4, F2, F1, and F0. [110]–[112] independently repeat the same first three result associations; [107] supplies the fourth. Thus the expression identities and final vector are stronger than any guess about what numerical values the glyphs encode.

The candidate identities are visible before the repeated attempts: A and B in [36], A and C in [40], D in [34]. Subsequent sequences preserve these structures while changing the agent argument. This supports an agent/candidate relation and progression among candidates, although not the exact English verb 'submit'.

Several distinctions must not be erased: F3 differs from F0 in argument order and final subexpression; F1-short lacks the second branch of F1; F4-short is not F4; some candidate spellings omit 𘃸 and inner grouping; some C variants end in 𗖎𘁡 rather than 𗹔𗄤; [110]–[112] use different outer operators despite agreeing on their result relations. These may reflect corrections, equivalent constructions, or agent mistakes. We preserve them instead of assuming all messages were correct.

Several leading lexical tokens also occur in argument/result positions: 𗈨𗣮 is a head in [13]/[15] but a result in [8]; 𘁹𘈪 is a head in [2]/[14] but a result in [39]; 𗽚𘜢 is a head in [37]/[110] but a result in [100]. This argues against confidently assigning each a fixed mathematical-function meaning. Some heads are favored by particular agents, but they are shared vocabulary: for example, 𘇪𗖭 is used by agents 6, 1, 7, and 4, and 𗈨𗣮 by agents 0 and 7. A simple sender-identity encoding therefore does not explain their distribution. Synonymy, ordinary lexical reuse, or context-dependent roles remain possibilities, not decoded facts.

What would change our minds: a lexical anchor could show that apparent index tokens are names rather than numerals, that 𗾮 is a role marker rather than a result/equality sign, that expressions describe records or propositions rather than programs, or that 𘔬𘏱 is not submission at all. A demonstrated rule for 𘃒 or omitted closing tokens could revise the grouping reconstruction. Shared characters inside two-glyph words alone are insufficient evidence for a compositional cipher; no reliable character-to-letter or character-to-English-word mapping was recovered. Most semantic vocabulary remains unknown. This is a partial structural decipherment, and the low-confidence task hypotheses should not be mistaken for recovery of the missing file.
